newsitem.title: GERMANY: German unemployment seen surging again in February.
newsitem.headline: German unemployment seen surging again in February.

text.p: German Labour Minister Norbert Bluem called on Sunday for closer cooperation between unions, employers and the government to fight unemployment which according to one newspaper hit 4.8 million in February.

"We must jointly pull ourselves together," Bluem said in an interview broadcast on Deutschlandfunk radio. The rise in joblessness was caused mainly by delays in implementing innovations in production and working practices, he said.
Bild am Sonntag said unemployment rose by 120,000 to a new postwar record of 4.8 million in February, lifting the rate to 12.5 percent from January's 12.2 percent.
In January the jobless total surged by more than 500,000 to 4.66 million, the highest level since Adolf Hitler's rise to power in the 1930s.
The paper did not give a source for the February figures which will be officially released by the Federal Labour Office on Thursday.

The unabated rise in unemployment with the resulting benefit payouts and loss of tax revenues has sparked fears that Germany may not be able to get its finances in shape for European monetary union, due to start on January 1, 1999.
Bluem said the government could not solve the problem on its own. "The primary responsibility for labour lies with companies."
Bavaria's finance minister Erwin Huber said in a radio interview on Sunday that federal government tax revenues in the first two months of 1997 were well below plan.
Meanwhile the head of Germany's DGB trade union federation, Dieter Schulte, said more than one million jobs could be created by combining various forms of shortening working hours.

Halving the number of overtime hours worked could create 370,000 jobs, raising the proportion of part-time working to levels seen in the Netherlands could lead to a further 490,000 jobs and introducing the 35 hour-week could create 570,000, Schulte told Focus magazine in an interview.
